title: The Missing Piece to Mini Whiteboards
author: Scientists in the Making
summary: This article identifies a critical flaw in standard mini whiteboard formative assessment: teachers provide feedback, but students do not apply it -- a classroom version of the question 'if feedback is given but not taken up, does it impact learning?' The author introduces Tick-Trick, a system developed from Carousel Teaching, in which students add checkmarks to each component of their whiteboard answer that the teacher confirms correct during a point-by-point review, then hold up boards showing their tick count for a second accountability scan. This forces active uptake of feedback in real time rather than passive listening and re-doing, transforming the formative loop from teacher-to-room into teacher-to-student-to-self. The author reports using Tick-Trick successfully in a complex stoichiometry unit where previous interventions left 50% of students still getting problems wrong after remediation; Tick-Trick produced audible 'light bulb moments' as students could identify exactly which step they were failing. The article also recommends Carousel Teaching as a professional development platform that models cognitive-science-aligned strategies through live classroom footage and think-aloud live modeling, with a multiple-choice quiz checking implementation quality. The broader implication is that any multi-step problem type (dimensional analysis, equation solving, proof steps) benefits from the Tick-Trick accountability structure because it localizes error at the step level rather than leaving students to guess what went wrong.
points: Mini whiteboards lose their formative value when the feedback loop stops at the teacher -- Tick-Trick closes the loop by requiring students to mark each correct component in real time, transforming passive feedback reception into active error-correction.

Scanning the room with exaggerated body language communicates to all students that every whiteboard matters, preventing the disengagement that occurs when teachers give individual verbal feedback to one student while the rest disengage.

Having students write their tick count at the corner of their board enables a rapid second scan that checks whether feedback was actually applied -- creating whole-class accountability without singling anyone out.

The system works particularly well for multi-step problems because students can identify exactly which step they are failing (not just 'wrong answer'), enabling targeted self-correction rather than undifferentiated re-doing.

Individual commentary during the initial scan ('Great work, Angela!') should be avoided entirely at this stage -- feedback should be directed at the class as a whole to maintain universal engagement before individualization.
quotes: The problem with this scenario is that despite the teacher providing students feedback on their answers, students are not applying the feedback to their own work. It becomes a classroom version of the question: 'If a tree falls in a forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound?'

Tick-trick is a system that allows students to apply teacher feedback to their mini whiteboard responses. Once students show you their initial answers, you provide students feedback by asking them to 'tick' the correct components of their work.

A common practice that teachers do when looking at mini whiteboard responses is to comment on students' work... 'I thought feedback was important.' Yes. It is. But at this stage it is important to provide classroom feedback instead of individual feedback. Individual feedback allows other students to check out.

Notice that the teacher is using their body language to scan the room. You want to use your body language to communicate to students that you care about what they have written on their mini whiteboards. To communicate this, make sure to exaggerate your movements when scanning the room.

I was able to break down these concepts into steps and incorporate Tick-Trick to ensure that students are checking every step of the way. Students were able to see exactly which part of the stoichiometry process they were struggling in and quickly remediate it. I heard a lot of light bulb moments going off during Tick-Trick.

Carousel Teaching follows this process: It begins with detailed explanations of teaching strategies through live modeling. (No death by Powerpoint!) If you are not familiar with live modeling, it is an instructional strategy in which the instructor writes on a blank surface and does a think-aloud. It respects the limits of working memory which makes it easier to digest the information.
